discussions.name: NWS Seattle
synopsis: Post-frontal showers will continue to subside this evening outside of convergence zone activity. Precipitation chances will linger into Friday as a weaker system brings light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the Cascades. A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation this weekend. An active weather pattern resumes next week with a series of systems moving over the region.
hydrology: A strong frontal system brought roughly 3 to 6 inches of rainfall along the Pacific Coast, with up to 9 to 11 inches of liquid over the Olympic Mountains. While this caused rises to most area rivers, most remained below flood stage. The exception is the Skokomish River at Potlach, which peaked this afternoon just under Major flood stage. River levels should continue to gradually fall tonight, with the Skokomish expected to recede below flood stage by late Friday. Additional rises to the Skokomish are possible next week with additional incoming precipitation, but a large degree of uncertainty remains over the extended forecast.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: Post-frontal showers will continue to subside this evening outside of convergence zone activity. Precipitation chances will linger into Friday as a weaker system brings light rain to the lowlands and light snow to the Cascades. A weak ridge building over the Pacific Northwest will bring a brief break in precipitation this weekend. An active weather pattern resumes next week with a series of systems moving over the region.

sections.title: Short term (tonight through Saturday night)
paragraphs: The latest forecast remains on track this evening with no updates. Lingering light showers are possible into this evening across the lowlands and Cascades, particularly the North Cascades, alongside convergence zone activity. A Winter Storm Warning remains in effect for the Northern Cascades for an additional 6 inches of snow above 4000 feet. Additionally, winds still remain breezy this evening with gusts to 20 mph.

A shortwave trough will move through Washington on Friday, bringing another round of light lowland rain and mountain snow beginning in the morning. The Cascade Passes will see some light snow accumulations, generally 1 to 2 inches through Snoqualmie and Stevens Passes.

Conditions will dry out Friday evening as an upper level ridge building offshore begins to shift inland. Saturday will be mostly dry, with the upper level ridge overhead. The ridge axis will shift east Saturday night, opening the door for additional precipitation as the next system approaches the Pacific Northwest.

While astronomical tides peaked today, coastal flooding remains a threat for many areas heading into the weekend. Areas along the north interior coastline are favored to see the highest degree of coastal flooding over the weekend, with lesser impacts expected elsewhere.

sections.title: Long term (Sunday through Thursday)
paragraphs: After a brief break, an active weather pattern resumes by the beginning of next week. Guidance suggests an upper level trough offshore on Sunday, which could potentially spread some precipitation across the region. Another low pressure system is on track to enter the region on Monday, though models are struggling with the trajectory of the upper level low. The European model has the low moving onshore over Washington, while the GFS brings the low northward over British Columbia. Another break in active weather is favored on Wednesday, with an upper level ridge building over the Pacific Northwest. However, the extended forecast remains fairly uncertain.
While any incoming storm systems next week are not expected to be particularly strong, additional coastal flooding may occur into next week due to high astronomical tides.

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Most terminals remain VFR with localized MVFR conditions in post with isolated showers moving across the area. Few showers will persist across the area overnight.A weak system will bring rain again starting Friday morning, continuing into the afternoon hours. Reduced visibility down to 4SM possible in the heavier showers. Additionally, ceilings will gradually lower throughout the day on Friday with MVFR conditions expected by the afternoon and continuing into Friday night. S/SW winds 8 to 12 kt this evening will slowly decrease to to 4-6 kt Friday morning, becoming light Friday evening and overnight.

KSEA...VFR this afternoon will prevail into Friday morning. A weak system will bring rain by the afternoon hours. Ceilings will lower through the day on Friday, with MVFR likely by 18Z. Visibility may also be reduced to 4SM in the heavier rain. S/SW winds around 8-12 kt will slowly ease tonight into tomorrow.

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Winds will continue to ease this evening across the area with Small Craft advisories ending for the interior waters by late tonight. Seas will be slower to come down but should lower below 10 ft by mid- day tomorrow.

A weak system will approach the waters on Friday, though impacts continue to remain negligible. High pressure is favored to develop over the waters through the weekend, with seas and winds to ease, the exception is the Strait of Juan De Fuca, where a westerly push of winds is likely.

The next impactful low pressure system looks to move across the area Monday into Tuesday for the next round of headlines for winds, and seas look to rise, potentially into the 15-20 ft range by early Tuesday. Calmer conditions look to be favored into the middle of next week.

sections.title: Hydrology
paragraphs: A strong frontal system brought roughly 3 to 6 inches of rainfall along the Pacific Coast, with up to 9 to 11 inches of liquid over the Olympic Mountains. While this caused rises to most area rivers, most remained below flood stage. The exception is the Skokomish River at Potlach, which peaked this afternoon just under Major flood stage. River levels should continue to gradually fall tonight, with the Skokomish expected to recede below flood stage by late Friday. Additional rises to the Skokomish are possible next week with additional incoming precipitation, but a large degree of uncertainty remains over the extended forecast.

discussions.name: NWS Portland
synopsis: A low pressure system will bring another round of steady rain on Friday, with periods of moderate to heavy rain for some locations. Dry weather and offshore winds return this weekend. Active weather returns on Monday with rain and wind, with a break from rain and wind expected late Tuesday into Wednesday.

sections.title: Synopsis
paragraphs: A low pressure system will bring another round of steady rain on Friday, with periods of moderate to heavy rain for some locations. Dry weather and offshore winds return this weekend. Active weather returns on Monday with rain and wind, with a break from rain and wind expected late Tuesday into Wednesday.

sections.title: Discussion
paragraphs: Now through Wednesday night...Scattered rain showers will continue through tonight in the wake of a cold front that finished pushing through southwest WA and northwest OR earlier today. A trailing area of low pressure will move into the region Friday morning, bringing another round of widespread rain. While not corresponding to canonical atmospheric river dynamics, this feature will nonetheless be able to tap into the same moisture stream with westerly mid-level flow oriented perpendicular to area terrain features, promoting a stronger orographic enhancement of rainfall. In addition, model guidance is showing a clear frontal boundary/baroclinic zone on the north side of the low with modest frontogenesis and a clear wind shift (weak north winds on the north side of the frontal boundary with gustier south winds on the south side of the boundary, strongest along the central Oregon coast and over the southern Willamette Valley). This area of enhanced frontogenesis is collocated with moderate to strong Q-vector convergence Friday afternoon per GFS guidance, suggesting there will be favorable forcing for ascent in place on both the mesoscale and synoptic scale. Given the moisture in place, this means hourly rain rates could exceed 0.25 inches/hour at times along and near the frontal boundary, including over the lowlands (not solely over higher terrain where orographic lift will be favorable as well). The latest REFS guidance backs this up, as several ensemble members show hourly rates around or slightly above 0.25 in/hr over the central/northern Willamette Valley and Portland metro Friday morning/afternoon and then the southern valley late Friday afternoon into the evening as the front sags southward. Rain rates of this magnitude are high enough to bring continued chances for nuisance urban flooding in areas with poor drainage. This will bring an increased risk of hydroplaning for motorists due to ponding of water on roads. Be sure to slow down and never drive on a flooded road. As mentioned earlier, winds will become gustier along the central Oregon coast and southern valley Friday afternoon, however confidence has increased high winds capable of widespread tree damage and power outages will NOT occur with this system, as NBM probabilities for max wind gusts over 55 mph are only around 1%. Chances for gusts over 45 mph are also near 1%, except 5-10% along the central Oregon coast to the south of Lincoln City.

Brief and transient upper-level ridging passes overhead on Saturday, favoring drier weather with offshore flow to begin the weekend. East winds are expected to peak Saturday night into Sunday morning in the Cascades and typical east-west oriented terrain gaps including the Columbia River Gorge. Expect the pressure gradient to peak around -4 to -5 mb between Troutdale and the Dalles, which should support peak gusts in the Gorge of 40-50 mph, and 20-30 mph in the eastern Portland/Vancouver metro. A small handful of EURO members show peak gradients near -6 to -8 mb, which would result in even stronger winds, however this is not the most likely outcome. There is good consensus that wet weather returns Sunday into Monday as chances for precipitation increase to around 90%, although the details of the synoptic pattern remain uncertain at this lead time. Snow levels are expected to trend downward, perhaps near 5000 feet by Monday night, which may allow for some light snow at the Cascade Passes, but that aspect of the forecast is also low confidence. Drier conditions likely return late Tuesday into Wednesday as the progressive pattern of recent weeks continues overhead. -23/36

sections.title: Aviation
paragraphs: Through 00z Saturday...Rain showers linger at times through the evening hours with a mix of MVFR to VFR CIGs likely at times. However, Cigs likely trend more towards MVFR by 08-12z Fri as low stratus develops overnight, then additional rainfall begins to increase from south to north Friday morning with higher chances for widespread MVFR conditions (50-80%). Will see increasing probabilities for IFR conditions on Friday as well, mainly late morning through the afternoon. Winds generally remain below 10-15 knots.
KPDX AND APPROACHES...Conditions remain a mix of VFR to MVFR late this afternoon, although it likely trends towards the latter Friday morning. Winds stay fairly light. -99

sections.title: Marine
paragraphs: Our latest weather system has passed out of the area to the east with decreasing winds and dissipating waves the rest of the evening. Current buoy observations show wave heights have decreased to 13-16ft with this trend holding going forward. Hazardous Seas Warnings remain in effect across the waters through 1 AM Friday as seas steadily ease to below 15 ft. From this point forward, Small Craft Advisories will then be in effect through 1 AM Saturday until seas fall below 10 ft. There continues to be a 10-20% chance that another area of surface low pressure moving onshore over the central Oregon coast on Friday, which should this occur would be strong enough to produce another round of gales south of Cape Lookout, but this is not the most likely scenario for tomorrow. Otherwise a brief break in the active weather will see calmer marine conditions on Saturday into early Sunday. However, the progressive weather pattern is very likely to usher in additional weather systems into the region early next week. Confidence is high (60-70%) wave heights exceed 15ft again late Monday into Tuesday. -99/36

sections.title: Beach hazards
paragraphs: The combination of King Tides and elevated seas leading to tidal overflow continue to support a Coastal Flood Advisory through Friday for the south Washington coast. Impacts during this period are most likely in the hours around high tide. Coastal residents in the warned area should be alert for rising water, and take appropriate action to protect life and property. There is also a continued moderate to high sneaker wave threat through Friday as well. Beachgoers should exercise caution, stay far back from incoming waves, and remain observant of the ocean. Avoid logs, large rocks, and jetties.
